newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Feeling of change in air as Suharto reaches 76.
newsitem.headline: Feeling of change in air as Suharto reaches 76.

text.p: President Suharto celebrated his 76th birthday on Sunday after 30 years in power during which he has raised Indonesia from a poverty-stricken nation racked by internal strife to one of Asia's economic tigers.
The world's second longest-serving leader after Cuba's Fidel Castro, Suharto is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term in office at a presidential poll next March.

But political analysts say a feeling of change is in the air, with rising tension over disparities in wealth, demands for more political openness and the overriding question of a successor to Suharto himself.

"In terms of fostering long-term stability, promoting unity and economic development, he gets top grades," said Dewi Fortuna Anwar, analyst with the Centre for Information and Development Studies (CIDES).
"But in terms of developing the political system, the record is very patchy," she told Reuters.

A series of isolated riots and the most violent campaign in three decades leading up the May 29 general elections have focused attention on such issues as the wealth gap, frustrations with an autocratic political system and pervasive corruption affecting the man in the street.
The ruling Golkar won a sweeping election victory, taking over 74 percent of the vote.
Golkar was assured of victory before a vote was cast, but the minority parties and independent observers have cried foul, alleging vote rigging and buying and intimidation at the polls.

Loyalists saw the result as a vote of confidence in Suharto and the "New Order" government he formed after taking power following an abortive coup blamed on the Communists in 1965 which led to the downfall of founding president Sukarno.
Of peasant origin and rising through the army, Suharto has proved an adept politician very much in the Javanese style who has survived on the principle of divide-and-rule over the years.
But some analysts question whether he is fully in touch with the undercurrents in the nation.
"He is still in control in politics, he's still the old fox," one analyst said.
"I don't think he's out of touch, but I think he is more remote in the sense that no-one is in a position to tell him what's going on," the analyst added.
The government was "externalising" its problems, blaming the riots for example on shadowy dissidents or outside factors rather than looking inward to find the causes within the community.

Suharto suffered a severe blow in April last year with the death of his wife of 50 years, Tien. But he recovered and doctors who gave him a medical checkup in Germany in mid-1996 pronounced him to be in good health for a man of his age.
Some analysts say the death of his wife means there is no-one now to control infighting among the president's children who have fingers in many of the major business concerns in the country.
Given Suharto's age, the succession is a key issue for Indonesians and for the foreign investment community.

There is keen interest in who he will select as his vice-president when the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), comprising 500 parliamentarians and 500 appointees, meets next March to elect the president and his running mate.

While no vice-president has had a second term, some analysts believe the present incumbent, Try Sutrisno, has a reasonable chance. Another name is retiring army chief of staff, General Hartono, who retires this week to become information minister.
A senior Asian diplomat said Suharto would be working hard over the coming months to build a consensus with the powerful armed forces (ABRI) and the political establishment ahead of the MPR vote.

"What he would want to avoid is an alternative candidate being put forward. He will want to get a consensus behind the vice-president because his own re-election is assured," the diplomat said. "The most important thing is to win ABRI support for the vice-president."
But political analysts also said the fundamentals -- particularly in the economy -- set in place over the years should be strong enough to withstand a succession shock.
"The New Order (government) has set a course which I think is irreversible," said CIDES' Dewi Anwar.
